**Summary: Origin of RCC vs. Urothelial Carcinoma Within the Kidney**

- **Renal cell carcinoma (RCC)** starts in the cells that line the **renal tubules** — the tiny tubes in the kidney that remove waste from blood and make urine. RCC is the most common type of kidney cancer (~9 out of 10 kidney cancers) and is a true kidney tumor.

- **Urothelial carcinoma** starts in the cells that line the **renal pelvis and ureter** (the structures that drain the kidney), not in the kidney tissue itself. Although these tumors can be found up the ureter near the kidneys, **they are not kidney tumors**. They share many features with bladder cancer and were formerly called transitional cell cancer. They are treated differently from RCC.

**Summary:**

In a child under 5 with an adrenal mass and bone metastases, the most likely diagnosis is **neuroblastoma** — a rare, cancerous adrenal tumor that affects children ages 5 and under (most often infants) and can spread to other parts of the body, including the bones.

**Diagnostic methods to prioritize:**
- **Imaging tests:** MRI may be used as an initial test and to assess cancer spread; PET scans (combined PET/CT or PET/MRI) help locate cancer cells and are considered more accurate than either scan alone.
- **Blood/biochemical tests:** Used to detect signs of hormone secretion (measuring hormones in blood, urine, and/or saliva).
- **Biopsy:** Listed among testing methods for diagnosing adrenal tumors.
- **Genetic tests:** Relevant given hereditary conditions linked to increased adrenal tumor risk.

Note: Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) also occurs in children ages 5 and under but is very rare (~1–2 per 1 million people). Neuroblastoma is distinguished by its occurrence in young children and its ability to spread to bones.

**Summary for Discharge Summary – Adrenocortical Carcinoma (ACC)**

- **Presentation:** ACC is a rare adrenal cancer arising in the adrenal cortex (outer layer of the adrenal gland). It can occur at any age but most commonly affects children ages 5 and under and adults in their 40s and 50s. Approximately half of patients present with symptoms from hormone overproduction; others present with symptoms from tumor growth pressing on nearby organs. ACC may be functioning (hormone-producing, sometimes producing more than one hormone) or nonfunctioning. If caught early, ACC can be cured; if it has spread beyond the adrenal glands, cure is less likely and treatment aims to delay progression or recurrence.

- **Diagnostic Process:** Diagnosis is based on a series of test results, including general health tests, imaging tests (e.g., CT scan), blood tests, genetic tests, and biopsy.
